pos: n. (proper name; head of a family of Nethinims who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Gachar, perhaps hiding place or lurker; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Gahar is the head of a family of Nethinims, the temple servants who came back from the captivity with Zerubbabel: “The children of Giddel, the children of Gahar, the children of Reaiah” (Ezra 2:47); the same names recur in Nehemiah's copy of the register (Nehemiah 7:49). The Nethinims, whose name means given ones, were a body of servants given to the Levites for the menial work of the sanctuary; their origin is commonly traced to the Gibeonites, whom Joshua made “hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD” (Joshua 9:27). Their total at the return was “three hundred ninety and two” with the children of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:58). That Gahar's descendants chose to leave Babylon for a ruined city and a humble office says much. They were not priests and could claim no inheritance of land, yet they went up to serve in the house of God.

corruption_paragraphs: A culture that measures worth by status will pass over the Nethinims as the least of the returning exiles. Ezra and Nehemiah list their families by name, the same care given to priests and princes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every office in God's house is honourable. A day in His courts is better than a thousand, and the drawer of water at His altar is counted in His register.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family of Nethinims who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Gazzam, devourer, from gazam, to cut off, and the noun gazam, the palmerworm.
biblical_def: Gazzam is the head of another family of Nethinims in the register of the return: “The children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda, the children of Gazzam” (Ezra 2:48); Nehemiah's copy has “The children of Gazzam, the children of Uzza, the children of Phaseah” (Nehemiah 7:51). His name is built on the word Joel uses for the palmerworm, the devouring locust of the plague God sent on Judah. Whatever lay behind the naming, the family it marked went up from Babylon to serve in the house of God. The Nethinims dwelt in Ophel near the temple (Nehemiah 3:26), and when Nehemiah renewed the covenant the Nethinims were counted among those that “separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God” (Nehemiah 10:28). A house named for a devourer became a house given to God's service; Joel's own promise, “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten”, is a word for such households.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a priestly family that could not prove its descent)
etymology: Hebrew Chabayah, the LORD hath hidden, from chaba', to hide, and Yah, the LORD.
biblical_def: Habaiah heads a family of priests in the register of the return whose title to the priesthood could not be proven: “And of the children of the priests: the children of Habaiah, the children of Koz, the children of Barzillai” (Ezra 2:61). “These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62). The governor did not cast them out of Israel; he barred them from the most holy things “till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim” (Ezra 2:63), that is, until God Himself should give a ruling. Habaiah's name, the LORD hath hidden, fits the case: their descent was hidden from men, and only God could reveal it. The episode guards a principle that runs to the New Testament. No man takes the priestly office to himself; Christ Himself “glorified not himself to be made an high priest”, but was called of God.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family of porters who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Chatita', perhaps exploration or digging; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Hatita heads one of the six families of porters, the gatekeepers of the temple, who returned with Zerubbabel: “The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all an hundred thirty and nine” (Ezra 2:42); Nehemiah's copy reckons a hundred thirty and eight. The porters were Levites charged with the doors and treasuries of God's house, an office the Chronicler says “David and Samuel the seer did ordain in their set office”. Their numbers were small and their work humble, yet it was holy work: the door is where the house is defended from what is unclean and opened to what belongs. The psalmist chose that office over the tents of wickedness: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (Psalm 84:10).

pos: n. (proper name; an overseer of the Nethinims in Nehemiah's Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Gishpa', of uncertain meaning, perhaps caress or attentive.
biblical_def: Gispa is named once, as one of two overseers of the Nethinims after the walls were rebuilt: “But the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel: and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims” (Nehemiah 11:21). Ophel was the ridge south of the temple mount, close by the water gate, where the temple servants could be near their work (Nehemiah 3:26). Ziha's name heads the list of Nethinim families in the register of the return, so Gispa's colleague came of the chief house among them. Nehemiah 11 records the repopulating of Jerusalem: a tenth of the people chosen by lot to dwell in the holy city, and the willing volunteers whom the people blessed. Gispa belongs to the order of that resettled city, an overseer of servants, set in his place so that the house of God would be served without confusion. Even the lowest order of temple service had its appointed heads.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Johanan, who went up with Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Haqqatan, the small one or the youngest, from qatan, small, with the article.
biblical_def: Hakkatan is named in the list of those who went up with Ezra in the reign of Artaxerxes: “And of the sons of Azgad; Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him an hundred and ten males” (Ezra 8:12). The King James margin offers an alternative, “the youngest son”, since the Hebrew haqqatan means the small one, and it may describe Johanan rather than name his father. Either way, the house of Azgad, which had sent a large company with Zerubbabel eighty years earlier, sent another hundred and ten men with Ezra. This second return was smaller and soberer. Ezra gathered them by the river of Ahava, found no Levites among them and sent for some, and “proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way” (Ezra 8:21). Hakkatan, the little one, is a fitting name for a man in a company that went up not in strength but in prayer.

pos: n. (proper name; a chief who sealed Nehemiah's covenant; also spelled Halohesh)
etymology: Hebrew Hallochesh, the whisperer or the enchanter, from lachash, to whisper, to charm.
biblical_def: Hallohesh is one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the covenant in Nehemiah's day: “Hallohesh, Pileha, Shobek” (Nehemiah 10:24). The same name, spelled Halohesh, belongs to the father of a ruler who repaired the wall: “And next unto him repaired Shallum the son of Halohesh, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, he and his daughters” (Nehemiah 3:12). If the house is the same, its head both built the wall and sealed the covenant, and its daughters laboured on the stones beside their brother, a detail Scripture records without apology. The name itself is surprising, for lachash is the word for a charmer's whisper and for the enchantments the law forbade. A house bearing that name put its seal to an oath to walk in God's law, which is what conversion looks like in a family: the old name kept, the old ways renounced.

pos: n. (proper name; a chief who sealed Nehemiah's covenant)
etymology: Hebrew Chashabnah, the LORD has reckoned or thought of, from chashab, to think, to reckon.
biblical_def: Hashabnah is one of the chiefs of the people who sealed the covenant: “Rehum, Hashabnah, Maaseiah” (Nehemiah 10:25). The covenant bound its signers “to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes” (Nehemiah 10:29), and it went on to particulars: no mixed marriages, no buying and selling on the sabbath, the seventh year kept, the third part of a shekel for the service of the house, the firstfruits and tithes brought in. Hashabnah is a name and nothing more, but the verb in it, chashab, is the verb of Genesis 15:6, where Abraham believed the LORD “and he counted it to him for righteousness.” The covenant Hashabnah sealed was obedience; the reckoning his name recalls is grace. The two belong in that order, and not the other.

pos: n. (proper name; one who stood by Ezra at the reading of the law)
etymology: Hebrew Chashbaddanah, perhaps judgment or considerate judge; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Hashbadana is one of the thirteen men who stood beside Ezra on the platform when the law was read to the assembled people: “And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, and Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbadana, Zechariah, and Meshullam” (Nehemiah 8:4). They stood as witnesses and supporters of the reading, men of standing who by their presence declared that the whole people received the book. “And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people; (for he was above all the people;) and when he opened it, all the people stood up” (Nehemiah 8:5). The Levites then “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Hashbadana's single appearance is at the birth of expository preaching in Israel.

pos: n. (proper name; a priest who returned with Zerubbabel; also Ginnetho)
biblical_def: Ginnethon is a priest of the first return. He is listed among “the priests and the Levites that went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua” (Nehemiah 12:1), in the form Ginnetho: “Iddo, Ginnetho, Abijah” (Nehemiah 12:4), and the margin gives the alternative spelling. A generation later his name had become the name of a priestly house: “Of Iddo, Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam” (Nehemiah 12:16). And a Ginnethon, the head of that house in Nehemiah's day, set his seal to the covenant: “Daniel, Ginnethon, Baruch” (Nehemiah 10:6). The name passes from a man to a family to a signature, which is how priestly courses were formed. It stands beside Iddo, whose grandson Zechariah prophesied in the rebuilding, a reminder that the priests of the return were not only ritual officers but the households from which God raised the last prophets.

corruption_summary: The priestly lists are treated as bureaucratic debris; they trace how a returned remnant rebuilt ordered worship across generations.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 12 is a list of priests and their successors and is rarely read. It records continuity: names that came back from Babylon became houses that served in their courses and sealed the covenant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is generational faithfulness. What one generation restores, the next must keep; the house of Ginnethon served under Zerubbabel, under Joiakim, and under Nehemiah.
roots_summary: Hebrew Ginnethon, gardener; a priest of the return whose name became a priestly house.
roots_lines: Hebrew Ginnethon, from gan, garden.
Ginnetho, a priest who went up with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 12:4).
His house headed by Meshullam under Joiakim (Nehemiah 12:16).
A Ginnethon sealed the covenant (Nehemiah 10:6).
Named beside Iddo, the house of the prophet Zechariah.
